You will unload groceries the whole day!
Chef, but I thought I would be cooking.
You credited yourself with two non-existent abilities!
The ability to think and the ability to cook!
I studied very well at the culinary college.
And here is a restaurant, not your college!
Now go to work immediately, oguzok!

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you.
And where's the toy car?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: the comparative 'быстрее', often as an order
the comparative 'быстрее', often as an order

examples.trans: He drives fast.

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

examples.text: Давай работай быстрее, гости уже давно ждут заказ!
examples.trans: Come on, work faster, the guests have been waiting for their order for a long time!

meanings.note: the present tense is normally left out: я мэр = I am the mayor
Secondary conversational sense ('there is, there are') (present есть; у меня есть = I have) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
future: буду / будешь ... + infinitive

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.
You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('important').

examples.trans: It's an important question.
I have important business.

examples.text: Я тебе утром говорил: не торопись. Это очень важный вопрос.
examples.trans: I told you this morning: don't rush. It's a very important question.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('everything') (neuter всё) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('everyone') (plural все) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
As you all know...
Share with everyone.

meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (stem 'играть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to win', paired with 'выигрывать'.

examples.trans: You won't win this election.
We won!

examples.text: Паша, эти выборы ты не выиграешь.
examples.trans: Pasha, you won't win this election.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to cook; to prepare', paired with 'приготовить'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to prepare') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm cooking lunch.
Mum cooks well.

examples.text: Я уже не могу готовить, стирать, убирать. Я хочу на море!
examples.trans: I can't take the cooking, washing and cleaning any more. I want to go to the sea!

meanings.note: 'два' with masculine/neuter nouns, 'две' with feminine; the noun goes into the genitive singular

examples.trans: In two weeks.
Two houses.

examples.text: Я выйду отсюда через две недели. Я решу все ваши проблемы.
examples.trans: I'll be out of here in two weeks. I'll solve all your problems.

meanings.note: Declinable neuter noun meaning 'matter', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('matter, business') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('case (in court)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I have a lot to do.
How are things?

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: на днях = in the next few days, or the other day

examples.trans: Good afternoon!
I'll call in the next few days.
Any day now, on the website.

meanings.note: думать о + prepositional = to think about

examples.trans: I'm thinking about work.
I have no time to think about that.

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'quickly'.
Secondary conversational sense ('vividly') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Off to the archive, now!
Come here, quick!

examples.text: Лёва! Ты ещё здесь? Живо в архив!
examples.trans: Lyova! Are you still here? Off to the archive, now!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'here'.

examples.trans: I'm here.
We live here.
But we're in business here.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'so'.
verb: Что это значит? = What does it mean?

examples.trans: So you're not coming?
So that's it.
Then make sure he does.

meanings.note: emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.
Dad and Mum.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to go', forming an aspectual pair with 'пойти'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('expression') (to run for a second term) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm going home.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'college', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Maksim graduated from culinary college.

examples.text: Я отличный повар и закончил кулинарный колледж.
examples.trans: I am an excellent cook and finished culinary college.

examples.text: Я очень хорошо учился в кулинарном колледже.
examples.trans: I studied very well at the culinary college.

meanings.note: in the instrumental: 'кем ты работаешь?'

examples.trans: Who are your rivals?
Who's there?
Arkady Borisovich, who are your rivals?

meanings.note: connected with cooking or the kitchen

examples.trans: He showed excellent culinary skills.

examples.text: Я отличный повар и закончил кулинарный колледж.
examples.trans: I am an excellent cook and finished culinary college.

examples.text: Ладно, сейчас проверим твои настоящие кулинарные навыки.
examples.trans: Fine, now we will test your real culinary skills.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.en: to reward, confer an award on
meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'граждать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to reward'.

examples.trans: To reward for work.

examples.text: Поэтому я награждаю тебя важным делом.
examples.trans: Therefore I reward you with an important task.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'строение'). Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'mood, spirits' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Вот с таким настроением и иди к Аникееву.
examples.trans: Go to Anikeev in just that mood.
I am in a good mood today.

examples.text: С таким настроением, конечно, не будет.
examples.trans: With an attitude like that, of course there won't be.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates

examples.trans: I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.
Chef, I didn't take it.

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'существующий'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('non-existent').

examples.trans: A non-existent rule.

examples.text: Ты приписал себе две несуществующие способности!
examples.trans: You credited yourself with two non-existent abilities!

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'but', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо ещё.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need more.
I want to, but I can't.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: hesitation, at the start of a sentence
Secondary conversational sense ('oh come on!') (ну, папа!) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Oh, come on, Dad!
Well?

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: playful derogatory nickname used by Chef Barinov for Max

examples.trans: Runt, are you still standing here?
The chef often called the newcomer a runt.

examples.text: Огузок, ты официально принят в штат нашего ресторана!
examples.trans: Rump, you are officially hired onto our restaurant staff!

meanings.note: accusative/genitive его (него after prepositions), dative ему (нему)
Secondary conversational sense ('it') (for masculine and neuter things) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Grab him!
It needs a wash.
Four-eyes! Grab him!

meanings.note: + на: опоздать на работу = be late for work

examples.trans: Sorry, I'm late.
Won't we be late?
Vikulya! Sorry, darling, I'm late.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.
Secondary conversational sense ('very much') (with verbs: очень люблю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.
It's very hard.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

поднять.gloss: to lift, to raise; to rouse

meanings.note: 'поднять людей' = to get people moving
'поднять людей' = to get people moving

examples.trans: I'll rally people!
Raise your hand.

examples.text: А я глаза на это закрывать не буду. Я подниму людей!
examples.trans: Well, I'm not going to close my eyes to this. I'll rally people!

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'пасть'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to hit', forming an aspectual pair with 'попадать'.

meanings.en: to get to, to end up
meanings.note: как попасть в центр? = how do I get to the centre?

examples.trans: A firework hit the power station.
How do I get to the station?

examples.text: Скажи: салют попал в станцию. Три района без света.
examples.trans: Say a firework hit the power station. Three districts without electricity.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'этому').

examples.text: Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: That's why I'm running for a second term.
I'm tired, so I'm at home.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.en: to ascribe, attribute, credit to oneself
meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'писать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to ascribe'.

examples.trans: To credit success to oneself.

examples.text: Ты приписал себе две несуществующие способности!
examples.trans: You credited yourself with two non-existent abilities!

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'traffic jam, cork' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: To get stuck in a traffic jam.

examples.text: Шеф, простите, я попал в пробку.
examples.trans: Chef, forgive me, I got stuck in a traffic jam.
There were terrible traffic jams on the road.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'дукт'). Common masculine noun meaning 'product, foodstuff' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Fresh food products.

examples.text: Ты будешь целый день разгружать продукты!
examples.trans: You will unload groceries the whole day!
The guests need the freshest product!

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'стить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to forgive', forming an aspectual pair with 'прощать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('excuse me, sorry') (imperative: прости / простите) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Excuse me, who are you?
Forgive me.
Please forgive me.

meanings.note: работать + instrumental = to work as: работать мэром

examples.trans: I work as mayor.
Where do you work?

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been working as mayor for four years now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'раз-' ('apart, un-, thoroughly') indicates distribution or intensive action (stem 'гружать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to unload'.

examples.trans: To unload food supplies.

examples.text: Ты будешь целый день разгружать продукты!
examples.trans: You will unload groceries the whole day!
Suslan, unload.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.text: Слушай, Нина, это же тот самый ресторан!
examples.trans: Listen, Nina, this is that very restaurant!

examples.text: Мы рады видеть вас в нашем ресторане.
examples.trans: We are glad to see you in our restaurant.
They called from the Italian restaurant.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('oneself') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.trans: I feel good.
He only thinks about himself.

examples.text: А с Пашей я снова чувствую себя женщиной.
examples.trans: And with Pasha I feel like a woman again.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'today'.

examples.trans: I'm at home today.
I'll be there tonight.

examples.text: Виктор Степанович, сегодня никак не могу.
examples.trans: Viktor Stepanovich, I really can't today.

meanings.en: to chip in, to club together
meanings.note: colloquial: everyone puts in some money; скидываться на + accusative = for something

examples.trans: We're all chipping in for a present.
Let's chip in!

examples.text: Понимаешь, Аркаша, мы все скидываемся на этот кластер. Мне москвичам сегодня надо отдать сто пятьдесят.
examples.trans: You see, Arkasha, we're all chipping in for this cluster. I have to give the Moscow people a hundred and fifty today.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'bet, wager, dispute' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is a bet, wager, dispute.
I agree to this bet!
I will definitely win this bet.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'пособность'). Abstract feminine noun formed with the Slavic suffix '-ость' ('-ness, -ity') from the corresponding adjective. Common feminine noun meaning 'ability, capability' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The ability to think.

examples.text: Ты приписал себе две несуществующие способности!
examples.trans: You credited yourself with two non-existent abilities!
The ability to think and the ability to cook!

meanings.en: to put, to place in an upright position
meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'тавить'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to put', forming an aspectual pair with 'поставить'.

examples.trans: Where should I put the plate?
Put the kettle on the table.

examples.text: Успокойтесь, я ещё сделаю! Куда ставить тарелку?
examples.trans: Calm down, I'll make more! Where should I put the plate?

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('your') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.trans: This is your coffee.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.
Your boss is here.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: You're greedy!
Have you got any more?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: instrumental of утро used as an adverb

examples.trans: I told you this morning.
In the morning I work.

examples.text: Я тебе утром говорил: не торопись. Это очень важный вопрос.
examples.trans: I told you this morning: don't rush. It's a very important question.

учиться.gloss: to study, to be a student; to learn

meanings.en: to study, to be a student
meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'читься'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to study', forming an aspectual pair with 'научиться'. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.

meanings.en: to learn how to do something
meanings.note: Secondary conversational sense ('to learn how to do something') (+ infinitive) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Но вы же с ним учились вместе!
examples.trans: But you studied together with him!
Where do you study?

examples.text: А я всё выучила. Я хорошо учусь.
examples.trans: And I've learned everything. I do well at school.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'well'.
Secondary conversational sense ('good, fine') (as an answer) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
Good! Everything's fine over there.

examples.text: Хорошо, Виктор Петрович, я сейчас же всё переделаю заново!
examples.trans: All right, Viktor Petrovich, I will redo everything right now!

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'whole', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('intact, in one piece') (not broken) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я не могу гулять здесь целый день.
examples.trans: I can't walk around here all day.
We waited for a whole hour.

examples.text: Илья Олегович! Я не могу гулять здесь целый день.
examples.trans: Ilya Olegovich! I can't walk around here all day.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'hour', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('o'clock') (в два часа = at two o'clock) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I'll be there in an hour.
It's three o'clock now.

examples.text: Слушай, я уеду на полтора часа. Ты с Викой посиди, понял?
examples.trans: Listen, I'm going out for an hour and a half. You stay with Vika, got it?

час.governs: after 2, 3, 4 and полтора the genitive часа is stressed on the ending

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'chef' (head, leader, from Latin 'caput'); in Russian kitchen culture 'шеф' is the standard form of address for the executive head chef.

examples.trans: Cleverly thought out, boss!
The boss signed the order.
The chef is in the kitchen.

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm doing my homework.
I grew up here.
Chef, I didn't take it.
